Headline: 'car exports' became 'car making'. The source names the automotive sector and global value chains, not exports. The headline is still under 160 characters.

growth_story.headline: Czechia caught up fast in the 2000s on foreign investment and car making; since 2008, shocks and stalling productivity have cut growth to 1.3 percent a year.
growth_story.arc: Since 1991, Czechia's growth has run in three eras. From 1991 to 1999, income per person grew only 0.2 percent a year. It fell 11.4 percent in 1991 at the start of the transition, and a currency crisis in 1997 led to a recession that the OECD saw as a response to built-up imbalances. From 2000 to 2007, growth jumped to 4.3 percent a year as the country joined global supply chains, above all in car making, with large foreign investment in manufacturing. Since 2008 it has averaged 1.3 percent a year, broken by the global crisis in 2009, a long recession in 2012-2013 that the IMF linked to the euro area slump, the pandemic in 2020 and the price surge that followed Russia's war in Ukraine. The sources describe productivity growth that slowed after the global financial crisis and stalled after the pandemic, while labour shortages and demographics weigh on the outlook; over the last decade income per person grew 1.6 percent a year, close to the 1.8 of the decade before, and in 2025 it reached its highest level so far.

threads.title: Transition and the 1997 crisis
threads.text: In the 1990s, voucher privatisation left firms with scattered owners, and largely state-owned banks kept lending to them, which pushed up wages and the current account deficit. A currency crisis followed in 1997, and the tight policy after it brought a recession; income per person fell in both 1997 and 1998.

threads.text: The global crisis cut income per person by 5.3 percent in 2009. A second downturn followed: income per person fell in 2012 and 2013, which the IMF tied to the euro area slump and weak spending at home, at a time of heavy budget tightening.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up in 2025. Income per person rose 2.8 percent, the best year since 2021, as real wages kept recovering and households spent more. Exports and private investment were softer, held back by global uncertainty and rising trade barriers.

growth_story.tension: The OECD describes the economy as flat in 2023, and the IMF estimated only a small fall in output, but income per person in the data fell 1.7 percent that year. The gap points to a growing population: the OECD reports a large inflow of refugees from Ukraine. The OECD also describes impressive strides toward OECD living standards in the three decades since Czechia joined, while income per person has grown only 1.3 percent a year since 2008.
